questions.stem: An object moves in a circle at constant speed. Which statement describes the net force on it?
options: Directed outward from the centre, balancing its inertia
Constant in size and always perpendicular to its velocity
Constant in size and always in the direction of its velocity
Zero, because the speed of the object is not changing
questions.explanation: Uniform circular motion needs a net force of constant magnitude that stays at right angles to the velocity, which means it points to the centre. A force along the velocity would change the speed. A net force of zero would give straight-line motion, and there is no outward force in an inertial frame.

questions.stem: Why is a car going around a roundabout at a steady 30 km/h said to be accelerating?
options: The direction of its velocity is changing all the time
Its speedometer reading rises slightly on each lap
The engine must keep supplying a forward force
Its kinetic energy increases as it turns the corner
questions.explanation: Velocity is a vector, so a change in direction is a change in velocity, even at constant speed. The rate of that change is the centripetal acceleration, directed to the centre. The speed and the kinetic energy stay the same in uniform circular motion.

questions.stem: A ball on a string is swung in a horizontal circle above a student's head. The string breaks. Ignoring gravity's effect on the path, how does the ball move just after the break?
options: In a straight line along the tangent to the circle
Straight outward along the radius, away from the centre
On along the same circle until air resistance slows it
On a spiral that slowly widens away from the centre
questions.explanation: Once the string breaks there is no horizontal net force, so by Newton's first law the ball keeps the velocity it had at that instant, which is along the tangent. It does not fly out along the radius, because no outward force ever acted on it.

questions.stem: In uniform circular motion, in which direction does the acceleration point?
options: Away from the centre of the circle
Along the tangent, opposite to the motion
Towards the centre of the circle
Along the tangent, in the direction of motion
questions.explanation: The acceleration is centripetal, meaning centre-seeking, with size v²/r. A tangential acceleration would change the speed, which does not happen in uniform circular motion.

questions.stem: A car travels at 20 m s⁻¹ around a curve of radius 80 m. What is the size of its centripetal acceleration?
options: 4.0 m s⁻²
5.0 m s⁻²
questions.explanation: a = v²/r = 20²/80 = 400/80 = 5.0 m s⁻². Using v instead of v² gives 20/80 = 0.25 m s⁻², and dividing r by v gives 4.0.

questions.stem: A cyclist rides around a circular track of radius 40 m at constant speed, completing each lap in 20 s. What is her speed?
options: 13 m s⁻¹
2.0 m s⁻¹
6.3 m s⁻¹
4.0 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: v = 2πr/T = 2π × 40/20 ≈ 12.6 m s⁻¹, which is 13 m s⁻¹ to two significant figures. Dividing the radius by the period gives 2.0, which leaves out the 2π for the circumference; using πr gives 6.3.

questions.stem: A car rounds the same flat curve twice, the second time at double the speed. How does the net force needed to keep it on the curve change?
options: It becomes four times as large
It becomes twice as large
It stays the same, as the radius is fixed
It halves, as less time is spent on the curve
questions.explanation: F = mv²/r, so the force depends on the square of the speed: doubling v multiplies F by 2² = 4. This is why speeding on a bend is so dangerous: the friction needed rises much faster than the speed.

questions.stem: A bus goes around a flat, unbanked roundabout at constant speed. Which force on the bus points towards the centre of the circle?
options: Sideways static friction from the road on the tyres
The normal force from the road on the tyres
The weight of the bus and its passengers
The driving force from the engine through the wheels
questions.explanation: On a flat road the normal force and the weight are both vertical, so neither can point to the centre. Only sideways static friction between the tyres and road can supply the horizontal net force. The driving force acts along the direction of travel.

questions.stem: A 1200 kg car rounds a flat curve of radius 50 m. The road can supply a sideways friction force of at most 7200 N. What is the greatest speed at which the car can take the curve?
options: 300 m s⁻¹
35 m s⁻¹
17 m s⁻¹
6.0 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: Friction supplies the net force, so mv²/r ≤ 7200 N. v² = 7200 × 50/1200 = 300, so v = √300 ≈ 17 m s⁻¹. 300 is v², not v, and 6.0 is 7200/1200, which leaves out the radius.

questions.stem: Rain makes a flat road slippery, so the greatest sideways friction force the tyres can get is smaller. What does this mean for a curve of fixed radius?
options: The greatest safe speed is unchanged, as the radius is fixed
The car needs a smaller net force to take the curve
Heavier cars can safely take the curve at higher speeds
The greatest safe speed on the curve is lower
questions.explanation: The greatest safe speed comes from mv²/r equalling the greatest friction force, so less friction means a lower speed limit. The net force needed at a given speed, mv²/r, does not change with the weather. Rain reduces the grip available, not the grip required.

questions.stem: A 0.20 kg puck on a frictionless horizontal table is tied to a central peg by a 0.50 m string. It moves in a circle at 3.0 m s⁻¹. What is the tension in the string?
questions.explanation: The tension is the only horizontal force, so it is the net force: T = mv²/r = 0.20 × 3.0²/0.50 = 3.6 N. Forgetting to square the speed gives 1.2 N. Weight and the normal force are vertical and cancel.

questions.stem: A small mass hangs from a string and moves in a horizontal circle, with the string at angle θ to the vertical. Which relationship gives its speed v for a circle of radius r?
options: tan θ = v²/(rg)
sin θ = v²/(rg)
tan θ = rg/v²
cos θ = v²/(rg)
questions.explanation: The vertical component of the tension, T cos θ, balances mg, and the horizontal component, T sin θ, is the net force mv²/r. Dividing gives tan θ = v²/(rg). The same equation describes a car on a banked track at its design speed, with the normal force in place of the tension.

questions.stem: A mass on a string moves in a horizontal circle of radius 0.40 m, with the string at 20° to the vertical. What is its speed? Use g = 9.8 m s⁻².
options: 3.3 m s⁻¹
1.2 m s⁻¹
1.4 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: tan θ = v²/(rg), so v = √(rg tan θ) = √(0.40 × 9.8 × tan 20°) = √1.43 ≈ 1.2 m s⁻¹. 1.4 is v² before taking the square root, and dividing by tan 20° instead gives about 3.3.

questions.stem: Why are the bends on many racetracks and highways banked, tilted towards the centre of the curve?
options: So the normal force has a horizontal part pointing to the centre
So the weight of the car gains a part pointing to the centre
So gravity pulls the car down the slope and slows it
So the tyres press less firmly on the road surface
questions.explanation: On a banked surface the normal force is tilted towards the centre, so its horizontal component supplies some or all of the net force. That means less sideways friction is needed. The weight is vertical whatever the road's slope.

questions.stem: A banked curve is said to have a 'design speed'. What happens at exactly that speed?
options: The car needs no net force to stay on the curve
The normal force on the car is exactly equal to its weight
The car can take the curve only with maximum friction
No sideways friction is needed to keep the car on the curve
questions.explanation: At the design speed the horizontal component of the normal force alone gives the required net force mv²/r, so the tyres need no sideways friction. There is still a net force, because the car is moving in a circle. The normal force is larger than the weight there.

questions.stem: A car takes a banked curve at its design speed, with no friction acting sideways. Which force, or component, provides the net force towards the centre?
options: The component of the weight down the slope, mg sin θ
The component of the weight into the slope, mg cos θ
The horizontal component of the normal force, N sin θ
The vertical component of the normal force, N cos θ
questions.explanation: Only two forces act: the weight, which is vertical, and the normal force, perpendicular to the road. The horizontal part of the normal force, N sin θ, points to the centre and equals mv²/r. The vertical part, N cos θ, balances the weight.

questions.stem: At its design speed, how does the normal force on a car on a banked curve compare with its weight?
options: Larger, because only its vertical part balances the weight
Smaller, because part of the weight acts down the slope
Equal, because the car is not accelerating vertically
Smaller, because the road is tilted away from the vertical
questions.explanation: N cos θ = mg, so N = mg/cos θ, which is greater than mg for any θ above zero. The car has no vertical acceleration, which is why the vertical component balances the weight, but the whole normal force is bigger. Smaller values come from resolving the weight along the slope, as for a block at rest on a ramp.

questions.stem: A 1500 kg car takes a curve banked at 20° at its design speed. What is the size of the normal force on it? Use g = 9.8 m s⁻².
questions.explanation: N cos θ = mg, so N = mg/cos 20° = 1500 × 9.8/0.940 ≈ 1.56 × 10⁴ N. Multiplying by cos 20° instead gives 1.4 × 10⁴ N, which is the value for a block resting on a ramp; 1.5 × 10⁴ N is the weight alone.

questions.stem: On a banked track at the design speed, which way does the net force on the car point?
options: Down the slope of the bank, parallel to the road
Perpendicular to the road surface, into the bank
Vertically downward, through the car's centre
Horizontally towards the centre of the circle
questions.explanation: The car moves in a horizontal circle, so its acceleration, and the net force, are horizontal and towards the centre. A common error is to point it down the slope, as on an inclined plane, but the car is not accelerating down the slope.

questions.stem: When analysing a block on an inclined plane you resolve the weight along and perpendicular to the slope. For a car at the design speed on a banked track you resolve the normal force horizontally and vertically instead. Why?
options: Banked tracks are too steep for components along the slope
The car's acceleration is horizontal, so the axes should match it
The normal force is larger than the weight on a banked track
The weight has no component along a banked road surface
questions.explanation: Choosing axes along and across the acceleration means one equation gives the net force and the other equals zero. On a ramp the block accelerates along the slope; on a banked track the car accelerates horizontally towards the centre. The weight does have a component along the bank, but resolving that way makes the algebra harder.

questions.stem: Which equation gives the design speed v of a curve of radius r banked at angle θ?
options: sin θ = v²/(rg)
tan θ = v/(rg)
cos θ = rg/v²
tan θ = v²/(rg)
questions.explanation: Horizontally N sin θ = mv²/r and vertically N cos θ = mg. Dividing the first by the second cancels N and m, giving tan θ = v²/(rg). Leaving the speed unsquared gives an equation that is dimensionally wrong.

questions.stem: A highway curve of radius 100 m is to be banked so that cars can take it at 20 m s⁻¹ with no sideways friction. At what angle should it be banked? Use g = 9.8 m s⁻².
questions.explanation: tan θ = v²/(rg) = 400/(100 × 9.8) = 0.408, so θ = tan⁻¹ 0.408 ≈ 22°. Taking sin⁻¹ of 0.408 gives 24°, and inverting the fraction gives 68°. Using v instead of v² gives 1.2°.

questions.stem: A curve of radius 80 m is banked at 25°. What is its design speed? Use g = 9.8 m s⁻².
options: 18 m s⁻¹
41 m s⁻¹
370 m s⁻¹
19 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: v = √(rg tan θ) = √(80 × 9.8 × tan 25°) = √366 ≈ 19 m s⁻¹. Using sin 25° gives 18 m s⁻¹; 370 is v², not v; dividing by tan θ gives 41.

questions.stem: Engineers want a bend banked at 30° to have a design speed of 25 m s⁻¹. What radius should the bend have? Use g = 9.8 m s⁻².
questions.explanation: r = v²/(g tan θ) = 625/(9.8 × tan 30°) = 625/5.66 ≈ 110 m. Using sin 30° gives about 130 m, multiplying by tan 30° gives 37 m, and using v instead of v² gives 4.4 m.

questions.stem: A loaded truck and a small car take the same banked curve. How do their design speeds compare?
options: The truck's is higher, because its weight is larger
The car's is higher, because it needs less net force
The truck's is lower, because its normal force is larger
They are the same, because the mass cancels out
questions.explanation: In tan θ = v²/(rg) the mass has cancelled, so the design speed depends only on the angle and the radius (and g). The truck needs a larger net force, but it also has a proportionally larger normal force to supply it.

questions.stem: Two curves are banked at the same angle. One has radius 50 m and the other 200 m. How does the design speed of the larger curve compare?
options: The same speed
Half as fast
Twice as fast
Four times as fast
questions.explanation: From tan θ = v²/(rg), v = √(rg tan θ), so v is proportional to √r. Four times the radius gives √4 = 2 times the design speed. Four times would follow if v were proportional to r.

questions.stem: A bend's design speed is to be doubled without changing its radius. What must happen to the banking angle θ?
options: θ must become four times as large
tan θ must become twice as large
tan θ must become four times as large
θ must become twice as large
questions.explanation: tan θ = v²/(rg), so doubling v multiplies tan θ by four. The angle itself does not scale like this: a 10° bend would need tan θ to rise from 0.176 to 0.705, about 35°, not 40° or 20°.

questions.stem: On which quantities does the design speed of a banked curve depend?
options: The banking angle and the radius of the curve
The banking angle and the mass of the vehicle
The radius of the curve and the grip of the tyres
The mass of the vehicle and the radius of the curve
questions.explanation: v = √(rg tan θ), so only the angle, the radius and g matter. The mass cancels, and the design speed is defined as the speed needing no friction, so tyre grip does not affect it.

questions.stem: A motorcyclist takes a banked curve well above its design speed. Without friction, which way would the bike tend to slide, and so which way does friction act?
options: It would slide down the bank, so friction acts up the slope
It would slide up the bank, so friction acts up the slope
It would not slide, so no friction acts along the slope
It would slide up the bank, so friction acts down the slope
questions.explanation: Above the design speed the horizontal part of the normal force is too small to give mv²/r, so the bike would drift outward and up the bank. Friction opposes that tendency, so it acts down the slope, and its horizontal component adds to the net force towards the centre.

questions.stem: A car is parked, stationary, on a steeply banked section of a racetrack. Which way does the friction force on its tyres act?
options: Up the slope, stopping it from sliding down the bank
Down the slope, adding to the net force on the car
Horizontally towards the centre of the curve
There is no friction, because the car is not moving
questions.explanation: At zero speed the car is far below the design speed and needs no net force. The component of the weight down the slope would make it slide inward, so static friction acts up the slope to balance it. Static friction acts on stationary objects whenever they would otherwise slide.

questions.stem: A curve is banked for 25 m s⁻¹ and the road is covered in smooth ice, so there is almost no friction. A car enters it at 15 m s⁻¹. What happens?
options: It slides up the bank towards the outside of the curve
It follows the curve, because banking needs no friction
It speeds up until it reaches the design speed
It slides down the bank towards the inside of the curve
questions.explanation: Below the design speed the horizontal part of the normal force is larger than the mv²/r needed, so the car curves too tightly and slides down the bank. With no friction to act up the slope, nothing stops it. Only at exactly 25 m s⁻¹ could it follow the curve on ice.

questions.stem: Why can a banked curve not remove the need for friction for every vehicle that uses it?
options: Each angle and radius suit only one speed, and traffic varies
Banking only works for vehicles below a certain mass
The normal force on a slope is always smaller than the weight
Banking only reduces friction when the road is wet
questions.explanation: No friction is needed only at the single design speed set by tan θ = v²/(rg). Slower vehicles need friction up the slope and faster ones need it down the slope. The mass cancels, so heavy and light vehicles share the same design speed.

questions.stem: On a railway curve the outer rail is raised above the inner rail, a feature called cant. What does this achieve for a train at the curve's design speed?
options: The train needs no net force at all to follow the curve
The wheels are pressed harder against the outer rail's side
The force from the rails is perpendicular to the track, not sideways
The train's weight is reduced as it goes around the curve
questions.explanation: Canting the track works like banking a road: the reaction force from the rails tilts towards the centre and supplies the net force. At the design speed the wheel flanges need not push sideways on the rails, reducing wear. There is still a net force towards the centre.

questions.stem: Track cycling velodromes have very steeply banked bends. Why does a steep bank suit them?
options: Steep banks let the riders' weight provide the net force
Steep banks reduce the riders' speed on the bends
Steep banks make the riders' normal force smaller
High speeds on tight bends need a large value of tan θ
questions.explanation: tan θ = v²/(rg), so high speeds on bends of small radius need a large tan θ, which means a steep angle. The net force still comes from the horizontal component of the normal force, which is larger than the riders' weight, not smaller.

questions.stem: Students roll a toy car around banked model tracks of different radius r, finding the speed v at which it needs no friction. They plot v² against r and get a straight line through the origin with gradient 4.9 m s⁻². What is the banking angle? Use g = 9.8 m s⁻².
questions.explanation: From tan θ = v²/(rg), v² = (g tan θ)r, so the gradient is g tan θ. tan θ = 4.9/9.8 = 0.50, giving θ ≈ 27°. Using sin θ = 0.50 gives 30°, and inverting the ratio gives 63°.

questions.stem: In the toy-car experiment, why did the students plot v² against r rather than v against r?
options: Squaring the speeds removes the random error in the timing
A graph of v against r would have a negative gradient
Plotting v² makes the line pass through the origin by itself
The theory predicts v² is proportional to r, giving a straight line
questions.explanation: The model v² = (g tan θ)r predicts a straight line through the origin when v² is plotted against r. The gradient then gives tan θ directly. A plot of v against r would curve, as v grows with √r. Squaring the data does not reduce its random error.

questions.stem: A 1500 kg car takes a curve of radius 125 m at 25 m s⁻¹. What size net force acts on it?
questions.explanation: F = mv²/r = 1500 × 625/125 = 7500 N, whatever the bank angle, because the net force depends only on the motion. 300 N leaves out the square on v, 1.5 × 10⁴ N is the car's weight, and 3.8 × 10⁴ N is mv, its momentum, not a force.
